weighing.summary: Nobody gives one start for Hood's division; Hood was wounded as it advanced and filed no report in the Official Records, and neither does Law. What the record gives: Lee (report of Jan. 1864) has Longstreet's guns opening about 4 p.m. and Hood's infantry moving 'soon afterward'; reports of 8-9 July 1863 from the 1st, 3rd (Ark.), 4th and 5th Texas say the order came about 4 (three regiments) or 4.30 (one); Alexander puts the order about 16:15. These fit one window, 16:00 to 16:30; Kershaw (1863; ordered to attack when Hood was engaged, and moving about 4), Alexander (1877) and Wilcox (1877) have Hood engaged about 4, which points to the first step at or a little before 16:00. 16:00 and 16:30 are the two ends of the window, not rival starts; the picture is drawn at the middle, which no report gives. Law's 'near 5' (1887) and Hill's 'about 2' (1863) are contradicted by those reports. Class weighted, tier inferred: the window is read from hedged statements, none states it.
weighing.who: The best-classed writers are the regimental officers (Work, Manning, Bryan, Bane): they wrote within a week, stood in the line, and were ordered forward themselves, which outranks Lee (a commander's report of six months later, place and source not stated), Alexander and Longstreet (memoirs of 1878-1907) and Law (1887). Union officers are a check, not a measure of the start: Meade's dispatch and Chamberlain's report date the attack and the guns about 4, Cummins (124th New York) says he was attacked between 3 and 4.
weighing.when: Regimental reports: 8 and 9 July 1863, 6-7 days after. Lee: January 1864 (six months). Hill: November 1863. Meade's dispatch: 8 p.m. on 2 July. Alexander: 1887 and 1907 (44 years). Longstreet: 1877-78 (15 years). Law: 1887 (24 years). The owner's rule (a report of the time beats a later report, which beats a reminiscence) puts the regiments first and sets Law and the two memoirs of the hour of the order below them.
weighing.where: Work, Manning, Bryan and Bane commanded or served in regiments of Robertson's brigade in the front line, next to Law's left; each gives the hour of his own order. Alexander directed the guns that went into position with Hood and McLaws; Longstreet says he rode with McLaws's line. Lee, Hill and Meade were not with Hood's regiments, and Lee does not say where he stood. Cummins's regiment held a rocky bluff near the extreme left of the Third Corps line.
weighing.how_knew: The regimental officers knew by their own orders and by what they saw. Lee gives no source for his hour. Alexander says 'I think' in 1887 and 'perhaps 30 minutes' in 1907, so both are estimates. Longstreet's 'half-past 3' is the hour of an order he does not tie to the step-off. Law speaks of his own advance but writes without a report. Hill gives no source.
weighing.clock: All Confederate figures are on one army's clock; the Union witnesses (Meade, Chamberlain, Cummins) are on another. The reported difference of about 20 minutes between the armies' clocks is not applied: it could account for Cummins's 'between 3 and 4' against the Confederate 'about 4', and it is carried as uncertainty only. 'About 4' is read as 15:45 to 16:15 and '4.30' as 16:15 to 16:45, which overlap at 16:15.
weighing.independence: Work, Manning, Bryan and Bane are four separate reports from one brigade; they may share the brigade's orders and talk, so they count as four voices of one source more than four independent ones. Lee relays reports from Longstreet's corps and is not independent of them. Alexander's memoirs of 1907 build on his article of 1887: one group. Longstreet's 1878 text is printed again in the Annals of the War (1879): one group. Hood's own book (1880) says only that the decision to attack came about 3 o'clock; Oates's 1905 book repeats Hood's passage in nearly the same words and is not a second witness.
